t8-tilt: Tilt Is the Most Expensive Leak

Tilt is the collapse of decision quality when emotion overrides reason. Jared Tendler's core claim in The Mental Game of Poker: most players produce 80% of their losses in 20% of their Tilt time. No matter how good the technique, a tilting player executes his worst version of strategy — one psychological leak can cancel all technical advantages.
The Seven Types of Tilt (Tendler's Classification)

(1) Bad-luck Tilt — ignited by a Bad Beat, "why does it always happen to me"; (2) Injustice Tilt — believing the game is targeting you; (3) Revenge Tilt — locking onto an opponent you must win back against; (4) Can't-lose Tilt — escalating risk to recover losses; (5) Mistake Tilt — self-attack over your own errors, spiraling; (6) Entitlement Tilt — "I play well so I deserve to win", most likely when a winner loses; (7) Despair Tilt — giving up after a long downswing. Identifying which types you have is the prerequisite for intervention: different triggers and antidotes.

Type-by-type breakdown (trigger → response): (1) Bad luck — triggers: river outdraw, AA losing to a fish; response: recite "this landed in the 20% branch", use T1's variance language, no excuses, no complaints. (2) Injustice — triggers: consecutive coolers, three Bad Beats; response: leave the table 10 minutes, tell yourself with data that the distribution is uniform and the deck has no memory. (3) Revenge — triggers: humiliating bluffs or slow-rolls by a specific player; response: change tables or leave directly, clear that "winning back from him is a byproduct, not the goal". (4) Can't-lose — trigger: starting to size up near the stop-loss line; response: execute the preset stop-loss, the line is non-negotiable. (5) Mistake — trigger: self-blame after misclicking a raise or an erroneous call; response: accept on the spot that "the error happened", leave the fix for review, don't punish yourself at the table. (6) Entitlement — trigger: thinking you're better than the opponent yet losing to a fish; response: remind yourself variance doesn't know skill — winners get Bad Beat too. (7) Despair — trigger: giving up resistance after days of downswing; response: preset a "downswing battle plan" (move down, reduce volume, reinforce basic training), turning despair into an action plan. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker seven-type Tilt classification and intervention)

Almost every Tilt type shares the same cognitive fuse: mistaking variance for injustice. T1's variance theory closes the loop here — those who truly internalize "correct decisions also lose in streaks" see Bad Beats as statistical noise; those who don't light a match every time.

Tilt has physiological and behavioral precursors that appear before the decision collapse: heart racing, jaw tightening, leaning forward; faster actions (calling without thinking), starting to play hands you'd normally fold, bet sizes suddenly losing logic, wanting to "teach someone a lesson". Build yourself a "precursor checklist" and catch the signal 10 minutes before the collapse — that 10 minutes is the stop-loss window.

Example: After AA gets outdrawn by T9s on the river, you catch yourself raising K4o from UTG the next hand. This isn't strategy; it's a standard revenge-Tilt symptom — the goal has drifted from "make +EV decisions" to "win it back right now". Players with a checklist execute their plan (leave the table 10 minutes); players without one lose three buy-ins 30 minutes later.

Example 2 (mistake-Tilt cascade): On the turn you miscalculated pot odds, called a bet you shouldn't have, and lost the river. The next three hands are all decided with a "I'm so stupid" mindset — entering with 97o preflop, snap-calling raises. Mistake Tilt's horror is that it's motivated by "punishing myself", and the punishment is playing more bad poker. Response: admit the error on the spot and switch the self-blame switch to "next hand, fresh start".

Tilt's expected loss ≈ Tilt hourly rate × duration
Example: A-Game rate +8bb, Tilt rate −15bb, lasting 1 hour → relative loss (8−(−15))×1 = 23bb
If you intervene within 10 minutes of the precursor (leave the table, cool down), duration drops to 0.1h → loss about 2.3bb
Conclusion: the "investment return" of intervention isn't a feeling but quantifiable chips — every minute the precursor checklist saves translates directly into money saved. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker A-Game state management)

The standard intervention sequence: recognize the precursor → physical interruption (leave the table, 10 deep breaths, water) → recite the preset script (like "variance is performing; my EV hasn't changed") → if you haven't hit the calm line, end the session. The value of interruption isn't relaxation; it's wresting decision authority back from the limbic system to the prefrontal cortex.

Write your own Tilt file: your 2 most common types, 3 precursor signals, 1 intervention plan. Tape it by the screen or keep it on your phone — when Tilt hits you won't have the ability to design a plan on the spot; you can only execute one.
t8-session: Your decision quality isn't constant: focus, patience, and emotional stability are resources consumed over time. Divide your state into A/B/C tiers (A = best decisions, B = okay, C = leak-ridden). Session management has exactly one goal: play as many hands as possible in A/B, and compress C time to zero. One extra hour of C-Game often costs more than three hours of A-Game profit.

Pre-table warm-up: enough sleep? Any residual emotion (life stress, last session's bad results)? What's today's strategic focus? Pros warm up like athletes; entering the table with residual emotion is like bringing your own fuse.

Session expectation = Σ(tier hourly rate × tier duration)
Example: A tier 3h×+10bb + B tier 1h×+3bb + C tier 0.5h×−20bb = 30+3−10 = +23bb
If you end before entering C tier (cutting the 0.5h): +33bb — cutting half an hour of C-Game earns 10bb more
Conclusion: state stop-loss isn't "quitting" — it's the arithmetically optimal exit time. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker session management)
The Truth About Stop-Loss Lines and Taking Profits

Purely mathematically every hand is independent; "stop when down X" doesn't change EV. But the stop-loss line manages you, not the cards: after consecutive losses, Tilt probability spikes and decision quality drops — the stop-loss line (commonly 2-3 buy-ins) is essentially a "state stop-loss", forcing exit before C-Game. Conversely "quit early when winning" has no mathematical basis: when the table is good (fish present) and your state is good, a winning session should actually be extended. Stay or leave depends on exactly two variables: table quality × your own state, unrelated to the day's profit or loss.

Example: 4 hours into the session, you're up 2 buy-ins, but you've miscalculated pot odds twice and started checking your phone. The textbook answer is to leave — state has slipped into B-/C tier, and continuing is paying for C-Game with A-Game earnings. "It's a shame to leave while winning" is entitlement psychology, not strategy.

Example 2 (executing the state stop-loss): Your rule is "leave when down 2 buy-ins". Tonight you're down 1.9, then win an AA all-in, back to −1.2. The thought "one more orbit and I'm even" surges — but your heart rate is already up and you keep glancing at the clock. Per the formula: at this moment your state has slipped into B-/C tier, continuing has negative EV, and the point of the stop-loss is precisely not letting "so close" hijack decisions.

Example 3 (table-quality assessment): You're up 3 buy-ins, but the 5 remaining players are all tight-aggressive regulars and the one or two fish just left. Using the "table quality × state" formula: table quality dropped (EV down), so continuing is just donating to tougher games. The correct move is to take profit or move to a softer table — stay/leave always depends on the two variables, unrelated to today's profit.
Review: The Session's Second Profit Source

Within 24 hours of the session, do a structured review: mark the 2-3 hardest hands (not the biggest pots), write down your reasoning at the time, verify with range analysis or a solver; also review the psychological side — which moment your state dropped a tier and what the trigger was. Technical review improves strategy; psychological review shortens C-Game — together their long-term value is no less than the table itself.
Fatigue is invisible Tilt: research repeatedly shows sleep deprivation damages judgment comparably to alcohol. The late-night "one more hour" decision is almost never made by your A-Game.

Write down three hard rules for yourself: a fixed pre-session warm-up checklist, an explicit state-exit signal (like two consecutive calculation errors), and a fixed review time. Rules only bind when written; rules kept in your head get rewritten by emotion on the spot.
t8-bankroll-psych: The Dual Function of Bankroll Management

Bankroll management's mathematical function is bankruptcy prevention: even long-term winners can see variance create 10-20 buy-in downswings, and insufficient funds turn "bad luck" into "permanently out". Common benchmarks: 20-40 buy-ins for cash games, 100+ for tournaments because variance is larger. But its equally important second function is psychological: only when a single buy-in's win/loss "doesn't hurt" can you execute correct but high-variance decisions.

Playable stake limit: cash bankroll ≥ 20-40 buy-ins; tournament bankroll ≥ 100 buy-ins
True floor = max(mathematical benchmark, psychological tolerance benchmark), take the stricter
Loss-aversion coefficient ≈ 2: the pain of losing 100 ≈ the pleasure of winning 200 (Kahneman's prospect theory)

Kelly criterion (brief): f* = (bp − q) / b
b = net odds (win b when winning, lose 1 when losing), p = win probability, q = 1 − p
Example: win rate 55% (q=0.45), odds 1:1 (b=1) → f* = (1×0.55 − 0.45) ÷ 1 = 0.10, i.e. optimal bet fraction = 10% of bankroll
Practical conclusion: even a clear 55% edge, Kelly suggests only 10% of funds — and it assumes no psychological wear during downswings, so in reality people use half-Kelly (5%) or more conservative. It gives the mathematical ceiling; psychological tolerance gives the floor. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker bankroll quantification; Kelly 1956)

Risk-tolerance check (three steps): (1) would losing 3 buy-ins in one session affect tonight's sleep and tomorrow's judgment? (2) would losing 10 buy-ins in a row distort your strategy? (3) after a 50% bankroll drawdown, can you still play per plan? If any answer is "yes", your psychological bankroll floor is above the mathematical one — decide stakes by the psychological floor.

The Scared Money mechanism: when stakes exceed psychological tolerance, loss aversion (the pain of losing 100 is about twice the pleasure of winning 100 — Kahneman's prospect theory) systematically distorts decisions: draws you should call get folded, bluffing spots go timid, thin river values get checked. The opponent needs no hand reading — just pressure.

Example: A player with a 10-buy-in bankroll sits at a +EV table and faces a flop all-in coin flip (52% equity, slight favorite). Math says call, but losing would break him — he folds. One hand doesn't cost much, but "systematically abandoning thin edges out of fear" accumulates and turns a winner into a loser. A fully bankrolled opponent makes the same decision with no burden — that's bankroll as fighting power.

Example 2 (Kelly in practice): You estimate a real edge of 3bb/100 at 2/5; half-Kelly converts to an affordable buy-in count of about 30-40. But psychologically you start agonizing over single-bet sizing after losing 8 buy-ins. So your true floor is the psychological 8, not the mathematical 30 — staying at 2/5 means every decision carries a Scared Money discount. The correct move: drop stakes until "8 buy-ins feels like 30-40".

Example 3 (moving down IS profit): Your bankroll drops from 40 buy-ins to 18; the mechanical rule requires moving down a level. You execute — three months later you're back to 60. Meanwhile the opponent who held the original level went from 18 to 6 and busted. Moving down lets you keep running your complete strategy (protecting +EV); holding means every decision is discounted by fear. Moving down isn't admitting failure; it's protecting the environment where +EV can run.
Discipline for Moving Up and Down

Healthy take-a-shot posture: try the higher level with an explicit budget (like 3 buy-ins), drop back immediately when gone, no re-buying. The psychological hurdle of moving down is harder: dropping feels like admitting defeat, so many players cling to the original level after drawdowns until bust. Writing promotions/demotions as mechanical rules (move up at X, down at Y) and executing unconditionally is the only way to strip ego out of financial decisions.

Another high-frequency psychological trap is "spending winnings" (the bankroll version of Winner's Tilt): after a win streak you feel like you're "playing with house money" and risk appetite surges. Accounting-wise there is no "house money" — all chips are equivalent; winnings join the total bankroll and obey the same rules.

Bankroll and life must be physically separated: table bankroll is earmarked funds; living expenses go in a separate account. Someone playing with rent money has every decision distorted by Scared Money — you've already lost the psychological war before sitting down.

Self-test: if you lost 3 buy-ins right now, would you sleep tonight? If not, your stakes exceed your psychological bankroll — the true bankroll floor is the stricter of the mathematical benchmark and psychological tolerance.
Risk of Ruin: Turning Don't-Go-Broke into a Number

Risk of Ruin (ROR), diffusion approximation:
ROR = exp(−2μB ÷ σ²), where μ = per-hand expectation (bb), σ² = per-hand variance (bb²), B = bankroll (bb)

At 5bb/100 with 80bb/100 std deviation: μ = 0.05bb, σ = 80 ÷ 10 = 8bb → σ² = 64bb²
10 buy-ins (1000bb) → exp(−2×0.05×1000 ÷ 64) = exp(−1.5625) ≈ 21%
20 buy-ins (2000bb) → exp(−3.125) ≈ 4.4%
30 buy-ins (3000bb) → exp(−4.6875) ≈ 0.9%

How to read it: every additional 10 buy-ins cuts the ruin probability to about one fifth — the decay is exponential, not linear.
Honesty note: this continuous approximation is a lower bound. Discrete buy-in structure, the habit of reloading after going broke, and psychological collapse during a downswing all push the real ruin probability above this table — which is exactly why the 20-40 buy-in baseline above still has to be combined with a psychological floor. (Concepts from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.3 variance and standard deviation; Kelly 1956, whose fraction-of-bankroll result belongs to the same family as the ruin-probability conclusion)

Example 4 (one skill set, two fates): Alice and Bob both genuinely play 5bb/100 with 80bb/100 variance, and play identically. Alice starts with 10 buy-ins, Bob with 30. By the formula above Alice's long-run ruin probability is about 21%, Bob's about 0.9% — more than one Alice in five is permanently out of the game before her edge ever pays off. A thicker bankroll changes not one hand of your winrate; it only changes how many more chances you get to use it. That is why having enough roll is a skill you can improve independently of your play.

Risk-of-ruin quick reference (100bb per buy-in, mu=0.05bb/hand, sigma=8bb/hand): thicker bankrolls cut ruin probability exponentially. 20 buy-ins is about 4.4% and 30 buy-ins is below 1% — the mathematical source of the 20-40 buy-in cash standard.
t8-mindset: The Four Major Cognitive Biases at the Poker Table

(1) Resulting: judging decision quality by the result — a lucky misplay gets remembered as "bold genius", a correct call that lost gets remembered as "a lesson". This is the biggest contaminant of the learning curve. (2) Confirmation bias: remembering only evidence that supports your judgment ("he always bluffs" — when he was caught only once). (3) Availability bias: recent or most painful memories get overweighted — just got outdrawn by a flush, so you overestimate every draw's threat. (4) Sunk-cost fallacy: "I've already put so much in the pot" — invested chips no longer belong to you; calls should only be based on current odds.

Complete cognitive-bias checklist (8+, for self-audit):
① Resulting — judging decisions by single results
② Confirmation bias — collecting only evidence supporting existing judgments
③ Availability — recent memories over-weighted
④ Sunk cost — keeping chips you've already invested alive
⑤ Gambler's fallacy — "five losses in a row, I'm due" (confusing independent events)
⑥ Overconfidence — overestimating the precision of your reads and judgments
⑦ Hindsight — "I knew he had AA" after showdown, contaminating review
⑧ Anchoring — locked onto the first piece of information (like an opponent label)
Each has a counter: ① judge EV not results; ② actively seek counterexamples; ③ replace recent memory with long-term frequency; ④ ask "considering only now, is the money still mine"; ⑤ reread T1 independent events; ⑥ test confidence with evidence; ⑦ write the decision first, the result after; ⑧ delay judgment and re-evaluate. (Concept from: Thinking in Bets Ch.1-4 decoupling decisions and results)

Annie Duke's antidote in Thinking in Bets: "decouple decisions from results". To evaluate any hand, only ask: given the information available at the time, what was this decision's expected value? Results are only for calibrating probability estimates, never for judging decisions.

The relationship between decision quality and results (Duke's decoupling quantified):
Single result = EV + variance noise
Long-term result of correct decisions = Σ EV (noise shrinks with sample size, proven in T1)
Bayesian calibration: P(correct decision | lost) ≠ 1 − P(lost | correct decision)
Example: a 55%-equity call lost; P(lost)=45% — but this doesn't change P(correct)=55%.
Review formula: only update the "probability estimate" (is 45% accurate?), not the "decision quality" (is the 55% call right?). (Concept from: Thinking in Bets Ch.2 correcting result-orientation)

Example: On the river you correctly called a 2:1 pot-odds bluff catch (his range bluffed 40%); this time he showed the nuts. A result-oriented review writes "shouldn't have called"; a probability-thinking review writes "was the 40% bluff-frequency judgment justified? Yes — so the call was correct; this just landed in the 60% branch". Two review styles, two different skill levels three months later.

Carol Dweck's mindset theory mapped to poker: a fixed mindset treats losing as evidence of "I can't do this", thus avoiding review and strong opponents; a growth mindset treats losing as data for locating leaks, actively seeking discomfort. Combined with the three elements of deliberate practice — focused training on weaknesses (not repeating comfort zones), immediate feedback (solver/coach/review), and spiraling difficulty — the skill gap is fundamentally a practice-quality gap.

The last piece of the long-term mindset is process goals: result goals (win X this month) are contaminated by variance and uncontrollable; process goals (review 3 hands daily, zero C-Game in a session, learn one theory module weekly) are fully controllable. Watch the process; results are the byproduct — in a variance-dominated game this isn't chicken soup, it's math.

Beware "fake learning": repeatedly watching entertainment hand videos, only reviewing winning hands, bookmarking tutorials without ever practicing — these activities provide the feeling of learning, not learning itself. There's only one test: did it change your next decision?

Turn this chapter's four biases into a review checklist and run it every review: "Am I judging decisions by results? Am I ignoring counterexamples? Am I magnifying fear with recent bad memories? Am I clinging to sunk costs?" — the best tool against bias is a checklist, not willpower.

Example 2 (hindsight contamination): On the river you fold top pair to an all-in and the opponent shows a bluff. In review you write "I knew he was bluffing" — but at the decision moment you didn't have that certainty; hindsight is rewriting the record. Counter: write down your judgment and reasoning at the decision moment (even mentally), compare after showdown, and you'll know your true reading precision.

Example 3 (anchoring and overconfidence): Your first impression labels the opponent "tight-passive", and after three consecutive big bluffs you still respond with the tight-passive model — anchoring makes you ignore counterexamples. Meanwhile you're fully confident in your reading precision, yet stats show your river hero-call win rate is only 30%. Fix: add "invalidation conditions" to every opponent label (re-evaluate if X counterexamples appear), and calibrate confidence with actual win rates.

t8-tilt-q1.question: Tendler's core claim about Tilt is:
options: Tilt is innate personality and can't change
Most players produce most of their losses during a minority of Tilt time
Tilt increases aggression so it's beneficial
t8-tilt-q1.explanation: 80% of losses come from 20% of Tilt time — the cost of emotional leaks is highly concentrated, so psychological training has a very high ROI.

t8-tilt-q2.question: The shared cognitive fuse of almost all Tilt types is:
t8-tilt-q2.explanation: Those who truly internalize "correct decisions also lose in streaks" see Bad Beats as noise; mistaking fluctuation for targeted injustice lights the fire every time.

t8-tilt-q3.question: After AA gets outdrawn, you raise K4o from UTG the next hand. This is most likely:
options: A Tilt symptom: the goal drifted from +EV decisions to "win it back now"
t8-tilt-q3.explanation: The decision basis shifting from math to emotion (revenge/can't-lose) is the hallmark of Tilt. Recognizing this kind of behavioral drift is exactly what the precursor checklist does.

t8-tilt-q4.question: The standard intervention after spotting a Tilt precursor is:
options: Physical interruption (leave the table / breathe), and end the session if you haven't hit the calm line
Move to another table and continue
Raise stakes to find your form
t8-tilt-q4.explanation: In an emotionally activated state you can't restore decision quality by willpower; physical interruption is the only reliable tool. The plan must be written in advance; on the spot you only execute.

t8-tilt-q5.question: A player, after a Bad Beat, starts playing any two suited cards and frequently raising to "teach the opponent a lesson". This is:
options: Bad-luck Tilt; only better luck can fix it
Injustice/Revenge Tilt combined: the goal drifts from +EV to retribution
Despair Tilt; he should keep playing
t8-tilt-q5.explanation: Attributing losses to "the game is unfair" (injustice) while locking onto a revenge target (revenge) is a typical combination. The key signal is the decision basis shifting from EV to emotion — start the precursor plan then.

t8-session-q1.question: The core goal of session management is:
options: Play as many hands as possible in A/B state and compress C-Game time
t8-session-q1.explanation: Decision quality is a consumable resource. One hour of C-Game loss often exceeds several hours of A-Game profit; managing state is managing profit.

t8-session-q2.question: The true function of a stop-loss line (like stopping after losing 2-3 buy-ins) is:
options: Forcing an exit before Tilt and decision-quality collapse (a state stop-loss)
t8-session-q2.explanation: Every hand is independent; a stop-loss doesn't change EV. It manages you — after consecutive losses the C-Game probability spikes, so the stop-loss is a preset breakwater.

t8-session-q3.question: The correct basis for deciding whether to keep playing or leave is:
options: Table quality and your own state
Whether half the time has passed
t8-session-q3.explanation: Extend when fish are present and state is good (even if you're winning a lot); leave when state drops a tier (even if you're winning). Profit/loss is variance on display, not a stay/leave basis.

t8-session-q4.question: Structured review should prioritize:
options: The 2-3 hardest decisions (win or lose) plus moments your state dropped a tier
t8-session-q4.explanation: Reviewing by pot size gets dragged by variance; reviewing by decision difficulty targets your own knowledge boundaries, and adding the psychological review completes the loop.

t8-session-q5.question: You're up 3 buy-ins, but all the fish at the table have left and only tight-aggressive regulars remain. You should:
options: Keep playing; leaving while winning is a waste
Move to a softer table or finish — the table-quality change altered EV
t8-session-q5.explanation: Stay/leave only depends on "table quality × your state": a lower table quality = negative EV for you; continuing is grinding your luck against tougher games, unrelated to whether you're winning.

t8-bankroll-psych-q1.question: Besides preventing bankruptcy, the equally critical second function of bankroll management is:
options: Making single win/loss "not hurt", so you can execute correct high-variance decisions
t8-bankroll-psych-q1.explanation: When stakes are within psychological tolerance, loss aversion doesn't distort decisions. Under Scared Money your technique can't function normally.

t8-bankroll-psych-q2.question: The typical behavioral signature of Scared Money is:
options: Systematically abandoning thin edges: not calling what you should call, not bluffing what you should bluff
t8-bankroll-psych-q2.explanation: Loss aversion makes correct "might lose" decisions get avoided — the accumulated abandonment of thin edges is enough to turn a winner into a loser.

t8-bankroll-psych-q3.question: A healthy "take a shot" is:
options: Keep playing higher stakes while it feels good
Set an explicit budget (like 3 buy-ins), drop back immediately when gone, no re-buy
t8-bankroll-psych-q3.explanation: Budgeted attempts keep the variance of moving up inside your bankroll structure; "re-buy after losing" is the bankroll version of can't-lose Tilt.

t8-bankroll-psych-q4.question: The root reason many players refuse to move down after a drawdown is:
options: Moving down psychologically feels like admitting defeat, and ego blocks the correct decision
t8-bankroll-psych-q4.explanation: Moving down is a purely correct financial move; all resistance comes from self-image. Writing it as a mechanical rule and executing unconditionally is the only solution.

t8-bankroll-psych-q5.question: The correct understanding of Kelly's criterion and poker bankroll management is:
options: Kelly provides the mathematical ceiling; in practice use half-Kelly or more conservative, and psychological tolerance provides the floor
Kelly only applies off the table
t8-bankroll-psych-q5.explanation: Full Kelly assumes no psychological wear and precisely known edges; most players' real edges can't support it. Half-Kelly or more conservative balances growth and variance, while psychological tolerance (e.g. distorting after losing N buy-ins) sets the actual floor.

t8-mindset-q1.question: The definition of "resulting" is:
options: Inferring decision quality from a single result
Ignoring results and only watching process
t8-mindset-q1.explanation: In a variance-dominated game, a single result is almost unrelated to decision quality; judging decisions by results systematically contaminates the learning curve.

t8-mindset-q2.question: "I've already put 200 in the pot; folding wastes it" commits:
options: The sunk-cost fallacy: invested chips aren't yours; only current odds matter
No error — with that much invested you should call
t8-mindset-q2.explanation: The chips you've put in the pot are no longer yours. A call decision depends only on the current call amount vs equity and pot odds (T2).

t8-mindset-q3.question: After correctly bluff-catching and running into the nuts, the probability-thinking review conclusion is:
options: Check whether the frequency judgment was justified; if yes, the decision was correct and just landed in the low-probability branch
t8-mindset-q3.explanation: Decouple decision from result: with a 40% bluff frequency the call is correct, and losing 60% of the time is part of the expectation.

t8-mindset-q4.question: In variance-dominated poker, you should set goals as:
options: Controllable process goals (review count, state management, learning progress)
t8-mindset-q4.explanation: Result goals are contaminated by variance and uncontrollable; chasing them necessarily triggers emotional swings. Process goals are fully controllable, and results are their long-term byproduct.

t8-mindset-q5.question: After the showdown you write "I knew he had AA; I shouldn't have called". This most likely reflects:
options: Hindsight bias: using the showdown result to rewrite the information state at decision time
t8-mindset-q5.explanation: At the decision moment you didn't know he had AA, otherwise the call's EV would be negative. Hindsight distorts review — the correct practice is recording the judgment before deciding and comparing after showdown to verify true precision.

t8-tilt-q6.question: You normally make +8bb per hand but lose 15bb per hand on tilt, playing about 30 hands an hour. The expected loss of one tilted hour is about:
t8-tilt-q6.explanation: The per-hand swing is 8−(−15)=23bb, times 30 hands equals 690bb. Tilt loss = state gap × hands played, which is exactly why early interruption pays.

t8-tilt-q7.question: The shared cognitive error behind most tilt episodes is:
t8-tilt-q7.explanation: A bad beat is statistical noise, but players who have not accepted variance read it as injustice. Restating results in variance language is the first step to defusing tilt.

t8-tilt-q8.question: The standard tilt intervention sequence is:
options: spot the warning signs → physical break → repeat a scripted line → end the session if still not calm
t8-tilt-q8.explanation: A break returns decision authority from the limbic system to the prefrontal cortex. Playing on, raising stakes or switching tables cannot fix a state already out of control.

t8-session-q6.question: The correct way to compute session EV is:
options: sum each state's hourly rate times its duration
record the day's win or loss directly
t8-session-q6.explanation: State is a resource: A-Game, fatigue and tilt have different hourly rates. Session EV = sum(state rate × duration); using the A-Game rate overestimates every session.

t8-session-q7.question: The right criterion for leaving a table is:
options: whether you are up on the day
whether you just lost a big pot
table quality and current state, not daily profit
whether a fixed number of hours has passed
t8-session-q7.explanation: Daily profit is a result and cannot guide staying. Leave when table quality or your state degrades; staying because you have not won it back is the doorway to tilt.

t8-session-q8.question: Which statement about fatigue and decisions is correct?
options: fatigue only affects stamina, not judgment
sleep loss impairs judgment comparably to alcohol
t8-session-q8.explanation: Research repeatedly shows sleep loss damages judgment like alcohol. The late-night one-more-hour decision is almost never made by A-Game, making fatigue a hidden tilt.

t8-bankroll-psych-q6.question: The common cash-game bankroll standard is:
t8-bankroll-psych-q6.explanation: Cash games usually require 20-40 buy-ins and tournaments 100+. The bankroll must absorb normal downswings, or scared money distorts decisions.

t8-bankroll-psych-q7.question: With a 55% win rate at even odds, the Kelly stake is:
t8-bankroll-psych-q7.explanation: f* = (bp − q)/b = (1×0.55 − 0.45)/1 = 0.10, or 10%; practical play usually uses half Kelly (5%) to reduce variance.

t8-bankroll-psych-q8.question: The typical distortion of scared money is:
options: folding draws that should call, backing off bluffs and checking rivers that deserve thin value
t8-bankroll-psych-q8.explanation: When stakes exceed psychological tolerance, loss aversion systematically biases play toward passivity. Opponents do not need reads, only sustained pressure.

t8-mindset-q6.question: Annie Duke's decoupling of decisions from results says:
options: judge a decision only with information available at the time
a winning decision is a good decision
a losing decision must be changed
t8-mindset-q6.explanation: Result = decision + variance. A decision can only be judged with the information available then; results calibrate probability estimates but never judge decisions.

t8-mindset-q7.question: Saying after showdown that you knew they had AA is which bias?
t8-mindset-q7.explanation: Hindsight bias overestimates how accurately you predicted before knowing the result. It corrupts review by making the process look better than it was.

t8-mindset-q8.question: The only test of whether a learning activity is real learning is:
options: whether it changed your next decision
t8-mindset-q8.explanation: Watching entertainment hands, reviewing only wins or hoarding tutorials can all simulate learning. Real learning is judged by behavior change: is the next similar decision different?
